lede: A farmer's son from the Ukrainian steppe who led the uprising that put Lenin in power, built the Red Army from nothing, lost the struggle for Lenin's place to Stalin, and was hunted across the world until an assassin reached him in a garden in Mexico.

ps: Lev Davidovich Bronstein was born on 7 November 1879 in Yanovka, in Kherson province in today's Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire. He took the name Trotsky in 1902.

He was a brilliant speaker and writer and one of the two leading figures of the October Revolution of 1917, with Lenin. As People's Commissar for War he built the Red Army and led it to victory in the Russian Civil War.

After Lenin's death he lost a power struggle with Stalin, was expelled from the party and the country, and spent eleven years in exile attacking Stalin's regime. A Soviet agent killed him in Mexico City in August 1940.
His parents were Jewish farmers who had done well on rented land. At about nine he was sent to school in Odessa, a busy port city, where he was top of his class.
In the town of Nikolaev, as a teenager, he joined a circle of young radicals and helped found a workers' union. He was arrested in 1898 and spent two years in prisons.
In prison he married a fellow revolutionary, Alexandra Sokolovskaya, and they were exiled together to Siberia, where they had two daughters.

ps.t: In 1902 he escaped, hidden under hay in a cart, and wrote the name Trotsky on a forged passport. It was reportedly the surname of one of his former jailers in Odessa.
ps.why: This comes from his autobiography, My Life (1930).

ps: London, 1902: he joined Lenin and the editors of the Marxist paper Iskra. At the party split of 1903 he sided against Lenin, and stayed outside both factions for years.

1905: during the revolution of that year he became chairman of the St Petersburg Soviet, the workers' council, at 26. He was arrested, tried and sentenced to exile in Siberia, and escaped again on the way.
1907 to 1917: years of exile in Vienna, Paris and finally New York, writing and arguing for his theory of 'permanent revolution', first set out in 1906.

1917: he returned to Russia in May, joined Lenin's Bolsheviks in the summer and in September became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet. Through its Military Revolutionary Committee he organised the seizure of power on 25 October.
1918: as foreign commissar he led the peace talks with Germany at Brest-Litovsk, tried to stall with 'neither war nor peace', and failed. Russia signed a harsh treaty in March.

1918 to 1925: as Commissar for War he built the Red Army, using former tsarist officers watched by political commissars and enforcing discipline with executions. He crossed the fronts in an armoured train.

March 1921: sailors at the Kronstadt naval base rebelled, demanding free elections to the soviets. He issued the ultimatum, and the Red Army stormed the fortress over the ice. Many rebels were shot afterwards.
1923 to 1927: after Lenin fell ill, Stalin, Zinoviev and Kamenev united against him. He lost his post at the War Commissariat in 1925 and was expelled from the party in November 1927.
1928 and 1929: he was exiled to Alma-Ata in Kazakhstan, then deported to Turkey, where he lived on the island of Prinkipo near Istanbul. He then moved to France and Norway.

1936 to 1938: at the Moscow show trials he was condemned in his absence as the chief plotter. In 1937 a commission led by the American philosopher John Dewey held hearings in Mexico, examined the charges and found him not guilty.
Mexico, January 1937: with the help of the painter Diego Rivera he was given asylum and lived in the Blue House of Frida Kahlo in Coyoacan, then in a fortified house nearby.
May 1940: a gang of Stalinist gunmen led by the painter David Alfaro Siqueiros sprayed his bedroom with bullets. He and his wife survived by hiding under the bed.

20 August 1940: Ramon Mercader, a Spanish communist working for Soviet intelligence, who had won the trust of the household under a false name, struck him on the head with an ice axe in his study. He died the next day, 21 August, aged 60.
1905 (1909), his account of the first Russian revolution.
Terrorism and Communism (1920), a defence of the Red Terror and of revolutionary violence against critics on the left.
Literature and Revolution (1924), on art and culture after the revolution.
My Life (1930), his autobiography, written on Prinkipo.
The History of the Russian Revolution (1930 to 1932), a vivid three-volume account of 1917 by one of its leaders.
The Revolution Betrayed (1936), arguing that the Soviet Union had fallen into the hands of a privileged bureaucracy.
Vladimir Lenin (1870 to 1924), first his opponent, then his partner in 1917.
Joseph Stalin (1878 to 1953), his rival, who drove him out and had him killed.
Natalia Sedova (1882 to 1962), his second wife and companion from 1902.
His four children, all of whom died before him: his son Sergei was shot in the Soviet Union in 1937, and his son Lev Sedov died in a Paris clinic in 1938 in unexplained circumstances.
Diego Rivera (1886 to 1957) and Frida Kahlo (1907 to 1954), the Mexican painters who took him in. He and Kahlo had a brief affair in 1937, and he later broke with Rivera.
Ramon Mercader (1913 to 1978), his killer, who served twenty years in a Mexican prison and was later honoured in the Soviet Union.

The Russian Empire was the largest state on earth, ruled by a tsar, with a fast-growing industrial working class and a mass of poor peasants. Jews faced legal limits and violent pogroms, which drew many young Jews to revolutionary movements.
The First World War broke the empire. After 1917 came a civil war of extreme cruelty on all sides, with famine and terror.
In the 1930s, as Stalin's purges reached abroad, many of Trotsky's supporters, secretaries and relatives were killed in the Soviet Union, Spain and France.
In 1938 he founded the Fourth International, a world network of small parties opposed to both capitalism and Stalinism. 'Trotskyist' groups still exist in many countries.
For decades the Soviet Union erased him from its history books and photographs.
His house in Coyoacan is now a museum, with bullet holes still in the bedroom walls, and his grave in the garden.

Historians still argue over him. Some see a brilliant revolutionary who might have led the Soviet Union differently. Others point out that he helped build the one-party state and used terror himself before Stalin turned it on him.

myths.c: He was killed with an ice pick.
myths.t: The weapon was a mountaineer's ice axe with a shortened handle, not the small pick used to break ice. Many accounts in English call it an ice pick.

myths.c: Lenin chose him as his heir.
myths.t: In his 'testament' of 1922 to 1923 Lenin called him perhaps the most able man in the leadership but criticised his excessive self-confidence. Lenin's sharpest words were for Stalin, whom he wanted removed. He named no successor.

myths.c: He was a gentle democrat betrayed by Stalin.
myths.t: He defended the Red Terror, took hostages in the civil war, and ordered the crushing of Kronstadt. He opposed Stalin's rule but defended the one-party system until near the end.

myths.c: Mercader was just a lone fanatic.
myths.t: He was an agent of the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, acting on orders that came from Stalin. His mother, Caridad, was also an agent and waited nearby during the attack.
